dimensions.form: Phrase headed immediately by a VP, optionally with a Subject; the VP is ultimately headed by V
dimensions.meaning: Clause-level content organized around the situation profile of the VP and, when expressed, its Subject
dimensions.function: Main or subordinate predication; argument, complement, modifier, supplement, or complete utterance where licensed
dimensions.distribution: Occurs independently and in the dependent positions licensed for finite and non-finite Clauses

1.definition: A Phrase whose Head is a VP and whose Subject is optional
1.details: Clause is defined here without exception as a headed Phrase. Its immediate Head is VP and its ultimate Head is V. An overt Subject, when present, is a Clause-level dependent rather than part of the VP. Subjectless imperative and non-finite Clauses therefore satisfy the same pattern as subject-bearing Clauses. Markers, prenuclear elements, and other Clause-level dependents do not alter the Head relation. A constituent without a VP in Head function is not a Clause in this Constructionary; non-headed structures with clause-like interpretations are assigned to clause-analogue-001.

examples.note: Subject Kim plus Head VP left early
Subjectless imperative Clause consisting overtly of its Head VP
The matrix Clause has Subject Clause leaving early and Head VP annoyed Pat

constraints.description: A Clause must have a VP in Head function; a constituent without a VP Head is not a Clause.
The Subject is optional in the general Clause pattern and, when present, is a dependent of Clause rather than VP.
Clause-level markers, prenuclear material, and supplements do not replace the VP as Head.
A coordination of Clauses is a non-headed coordination, not itself a Clause.

projection.target: Clause membership predicts availability of clause-level polarity, clause-type, subordination, and information-packaging contrasts, together with distribution as a main unit or as a clausal dependent; the VP Head predicts the Clause's internal complementation profile
projection.evidence: CGEL's canonical and non-canonical Clause systems preserve the VP-headed organization across polarity, clause type, voice, subordination, and information packaging, while non-finite data show that an overt Subject is not required

grounds.note: VP-headed membership projects Clause-level systems and distribution beyond the Head/Subject diagnostics
VP-headed structure persists across major Clause contrasts; non-finite Clauses establish the optionality of overt Subject

known_boundary_items: Constituents that CGEL calls verbless clauses have clause-like interpretations but no VP Head; they are excluded here
Attributive VPs are VPs but do not thereby instantiate a separate Clause node

relatedConstructions.notes: Clause specializes Phrase with VP as its immediate Head
The Clause's obligatory Head constituent is a VP
Both can convey clause-like content, but only Clause is formally headed by VP
Finite subject-bearing Clauses provide the Subject–verb configuration in which number agreement is realized
A coordination may contain Clauses as coordinates, but the coordination itself is non-headed and is not a Clause

grounds.note: Clause is a phrasal category whose Predicate/Head is VP, ultimately headed by V
Subjectless non-finites show that an overt Subject is not necessary for Clause status
Clause is strictly a Phrase headed by VP with an optional Subject; there is no verbless exception

curious.title: What counts as a clause
curious.summary: In this dictionary a clause is a group of words built around a verb and what goes with it, with or without a subject.
curious.body:
A clause is built around a verb and whatever goes with it. Kim left early has someone doing something: Kim is who left, and left early is the verb part. Leave early! has only the verb part, and it's still a clause.

Clauses can sit inside other clauses. In Leaving early annoyed Pat, the opening words Leaving early are a clause that acts as the subject of the whole sentence. Short phrases that carry a message but have no verb part aren't clauses here, though they can mean something clause-like.
curious.try: Find the verb in a sentence you wrote today. What are the words that go with it?

teacher.summary: Defines Clause strictly as a phrase headed by a VP, which separates it from verbless structures and from coordinations.
teacher.explain: A Clause is a phrase whose head is a VP, with an optional subject. In Kim left early, Kim is the subject and left early is the head VP. Leave early! is a subjectless imperative: the Clause is just its head VP. In Leaving early annoyed Pat, the matrix Clause has a subject that is itself a Clause. The subject is a dependent of the Clause, not part of the VP. Markers and other clause-level dependents don't replace the VP as head. A coordination of Clauses is non-headed and is not itself a Clause.
teacher.terms: CGEL also counts verbless clauses as clauses. This dictionary does not: a structure with a clause-like meaning but no VP head is not a Clause here; it is assigned to a separate category, the clause analogue.

contrasts.note: Head VP alone, with no subject.

watch_for: A learner might think a Clause must have a subject, when some Clauses, such as imperatives and non-finite Clauses, have none.
A learner might count a verbless phrase with clause-like meaning as a Clause, when it has no VP head.
A learner might treat Kim left early and Pat stayed as one Clause, when a coordination of Clauses is not itself a Clause.
teacher.activity: Give students a mix of sentences and verbless fragments. They circle the verb in each, mark the subject when there is one, and sort the items into clause and not a clause.
